newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: China to make New Zealand-invented engine.
newsitem.headline: China to make New Zealand-invented engine.

text.p: A Chinese company is to manufacture an engine whose New Zealand inventors say it outperforms conventional rivals by virtually every measure.

"This engine scores on every single aspect you measure engines on -- it's lighter in weight, it's easy and very cheap to make, it's incredibly powerful, it's very low on emissions and it's extremely fuel-efficient," co-inventor Graeme Jenkins said in an interview with Reuters.
World patents and licensing rights are owned by a tiny New Zealand company, Continuous Cycle Engine Development (CCED).
In what Jenkins described as a multi-million dollar deal, CCED has signed a memorandum of understanding with China's Sichuan Donghua Machinery Works.
CHINA DEAL, MALAYSIAN GO-BETWEEN
The Chinese firm has bought the technology and the deal includes a licensing arrangement where CCED gets royalties based on the cubic capacity of each unit produced.
A private Malaysian company, Pacific Base, acted as go-between for CCED and Donghua and will form a joint venture to manufacture and market the engines in China.
Jenkins is scarcely able to contain his enthusiasm for the new engine, known as the Smitkin.
"It will change the world, provided somebody runs with it. Once one country runs with it, everyone else can't afford not to have it because of its advantages," Jenkins said.
"Until someone runs with it it is not going to change anything. Now that China has taken it up, everyone else is going to have to fall in line."
Pacific Base representative David Lau said licensing on a global basis would probably be looked at.

Representatives of the provincial and central Chinese governments recently attended a demonstration of the Smitkin in China and Donghua and CCED agreed to set up a joint research and development company.
LABORATORY TESTING
However, there has been little objective analysis of the engine and all testing to date has been in the laboratory on computers rather than actual tests in vehicles.
Two years ago Ford New Zealand assessed the engine and was interested enough to send details on to Ford in Detroit.
Ford NZ production planning engineer Peter Ludwig said initial inspection showed the engine "had some merit".
"We were quite taken by the demonstration but it was in the early stage of development. They needed more performance information to sell the idea to Ford," he told Reuters.
"It's intriguing, it does show promise. It warranted further investigation."

Jenkins reels off a mind-boggling list of the engine's advantages over conventional engines. Among others, it is compact, vibration-free, surpasses all emission standards and can run on a variety of fuels.
He says fuel consumption is about 60 percent better than conventional engines, it is air cooled and thus requires no radiator, and torque is such that vehicles would require fewer gears.

A prototype Smitkin made of aluminium weighs around 24 kg, against a similar 2 litre combustion engine of 140 kg, and is about the size of a car wheel without the tyre. The Smitkin diesel version has only 30 parts compared with around 2,000 in current four cyclinder diesels.
MANUFACTURING
Jenkins expects the Chinese to begin manufacturing within two years. Possible applications are diverse, ranging from marine and aircraft engines to power generation.
Eventually, the engines will be sold in the West.
Co-inventor Roger Smith came up with the idea over three years ago largely from ideas in his own head and the partners havve been working on prototypes since then.
The nearest thing to the Smitkin concept was a rotating piston engine developed by a Frenchman in World War One. There was little similarity with existing rotary engines.
Jenkins says he understands scepticism about the Smitkin.
"People who think they know engineering said it would never run but engineers from other companies come and see it and say this is the most incredible thing they have seen. It staggers them."
Jenkins said unbelievers were welcome to view a Smitkin on a test bed where it is wired to computers.
"Anyone is free to make an appointment and see us and bring their best, most qualified, cleverest engineer, and come to our shop and have a look. We have nothing to hide.
"The potential is huge."
